## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Algorithms for Network Optimization and Management
  Official title       Algorithmes pour l’optimisation et la gestion des réseaux
  Instructors          N. PERROT (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 30 h (lectures 12 h, labs 18 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label}[Track I&I]{.badge .track}
  Language             French, with course materials in English (master-mva.com) · Université Paris-Saclay: French, no distance learning
  Assessment           Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (non-integral continuous assessment) · master-mva.com displays no assessment modality · weights not displayed
  Prerequisites        Operations research, Python programming, networks (master-mva.com and Université Paris-Saclay)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who knows what a linear program is and wants to see how operators decide where to install capacity, how to route traffic and where to place network functions.

**Empirical first**: on the six-node backbone used throughout this page, routing each demand on one minimum-hop path loads a 5 Gb/s link to 92 %. A linear program routes the same 40 Gb/s with a maximum load of 82.1 %, and a two-link cut proves that nobody can do better. Splitting evenly over all minimum-hop paths, which sounds safer, overloads that link to 123 %.

The course is about decision support for networks. It turns design, planning and operation questions into mathematical programs, solves them exactly when possible and approximately when time is short, and then studies the new problems of virtualized and autonomous networks. It shares its duality and decomposition tools with [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) and [Distributed and Large-Scale Optimization](../s1-distributed-optimization/index.html), and its learning-based methods with [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html) and [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Describe a telecommunication network as an optimization model: graph, capacities, traffic matrix, routing rules, time scale of the decision.
-   Compute shortest paths, maximum flows, minimum cuts and minimum-cost flows, and explain why the last ones are integral.
-   Write arc-node and arc-path formulations of multicommodity flow problems and solve them with an off-the-shelf solver.
-   Formulate traffic engineering, network design, capacity planning and placement problems as linear or mixed-integer programs, and compare the strength of two formulations.
-   Derive valid inequalities (cut-set, metric) and lower bounds from LP duality and Lagrangian relaxation.
-   Implement branch-and-bound, a subgradient method, column generation and the principle of Benders decomposition on network problems.
-   Design, tune and evaluate heuristics, reporting a gap to a proven bound.
-   Model network slicing, online admission, resilience, security and energy requirements, starting from a written specification.
-   Explain how machine learning can speed up or replace parts of an optimization pipeline, and what guarantees are lost.
-   Read a research paper on network optimization, reproduce one of its results and present it.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com presents decision support as essential to plan and manage networks. Its objective is to give knowledge of mathematical optimization methods and of their use for network design and management, methods it calls all the more crucial as algorithmic challenges grow with virtualized and autonomous networks.

The first part refreshes operations research (combinatorial optimization, graph theory) and telecom networks, presents the main exact methods, applies them to network design, capacity planning, traffic engineering and placement of network components, and uses labs with off-the-shelf solvers and heuristics. The second part covers the optimization problems of recent network evolutions, with labs based on research papers. ### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: operations research, Python programming and networks. The course carries the I&I track label and is limited to 20 students (numerus clausus, master-mva.com).

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (linear programming, duality, convexity), [Scientific Python](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (NumPy, SciPy for every lab) and [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (for uncertain traffic in ch. 9).
-   **Semester 1 courses that prepare it** — [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (Lagrangian duality, subgradients), [Foundations of Distributed and Large-Scale Computing Optimization](../s1-distributed-optimization/index.html) (decomposition), [Advanced Learning for Text and Graph Data](../s1-altegrad/index.html) and [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) (graph neural networks for ch. 10), [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) (discrete transport is a minimum-cost flow).
-   **Related courses of semester 2** — [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html), [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html), [Stopping Times and Online Algorithms](../s2-stopping-times-online/index.html) (competitive analysis, ch. 8.3), [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html), [Graphical Models: Discrete Inference and Learning](../s2-graphical-models-discrete/index.html) (minimum cuts and LP relaxations) and [Artificial Intelligence and the Environment](../s2-ai-environment/index.html) (energy, ch. 9.4).
-   **After the course** — the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html), often hosted by operators, equipment vendors or operations research laboratories.

### Course outline

-   **Review: graphs, linear programming and complexity** — incidence matrices, LP duality and complementary slackness, integer programs, NP-hardness.
-   **Telecommunication networks and their optimization problems** — layers, capacities, traffic matrices, routing protocols, virtualization, and the three time scales of decisions.
-   **Flows, paths and cuts** — shortest paths, maximum flow and minimum cut, total unimodularity, multicommodity flows and their feasibility.
-   **Traffic engineering: routing the flows** — congestion objectives, the minimum maximum utilisation LP and its dual, shortest-path routing with weights, explicit and segment routing.
-   **Network design and capacity planning** — fixed-charge design, strong and weak formulations, modular capacities, cut-set and metric inequalities.
-   **Exact methods** — branch-and-bound, cutting planes, Lagrangian relaxation, column generation and Benders decomposition.
-   **Placement of network components** — facility location, SDN controllers, virtual network functions and service chains, virtual network embedding.
-   **Heuristics and matheuristics** — greedy and rounding, local search and metaheuristics, solver-based heuristics, honest evaluation.
-   **Future networks: virtualization, slicing and autonomy** — slicing models, online admission, closed-loop re-optimization, from a standard to a model.
-   **Resilience, security and energy** — survivable design, robust routing, interdiction and monitoring, energy-aware routing.
-   **Hybrid methods: optimization and learning** — learning to branch and to prune, with the guarantees that remain.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — fast and learned traffic engineering at scale, guarantees for heuristics, robustness from data, joint compute–network orchestration, language models for modelling, decision-focused learning (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1; the duality results are used in every later chapter without warning.
-   Keep the six-node backbone of ch. 1 in mind: it reappears in ch. 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 and 9, and its numbers can be checked by hand.
-   After each session, run the Python blocks of the chapter and change one parameter (traffic volume, capacity, number of candidate paths) to see which constraint becomes binding.
-   Do the ★ exercises the same week; the ★★ proofs (Ex. 7–16) prepare the written part of any assessment.
-   The Python environment is NumPy, SciPy (whose `linprog` and `milp` call the open-source HiGHS solver), NetworkX and scikit-learn. Commercial solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi) have free academic licences and solve the same models faster.
-   For the second part, choose a paper from ch. 11 early and read it alongside ch. 8–10.

## 0. Review: graphs, linear programming and complexity {#ch0}

Every model of the course is a graph with numbers on its arcs, turned into a linear or integer program. This chapter fixes the notation and recalls the three results used everywhere: the incidence matrix, LP duality and the meaning of NP-hardness.

### 0.1 Graphs and their matrices

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Directed graph, paths and cuts]{.tag} A directed graph $G = (V, A)$ has $n$ nodes and $m$ arcs. An arc $a = (u, v)$ leaves $u$ and enters $v$. A path is a sequence of arcs in which each arc enters the node the next one leaves.

For a set of nodes $S$, the cut $\delta^+(S)$ contains the arcs leaving $S$ and $\delta^-(S)$ those entering it.

Each arc may carry a capacity $c_a \geq 0$ and a cost or length $w_a$.
:::

A telecom link is full duplex: it is modelled by two opposite arcs with the same capacity, as in the backbone of ch. 1.

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — Node–arc incidence matrix]{.tag} The incidence matrix $N \in \{-1, 0, 1\}^{n \times m}$ has one row per node and one column per arc. The column of arc $(u, v)$ has $+1$ in row $u$, $-1$ in row $v$ and zeros elsewhere.

Arc flows $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ satisfy **flow conservation** with supplies $b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ when
$$
N x = b .
$$
Row $v$ reads: flow out of $v$ minus flow into $v$ equals $b_v$. Sources have $b_v > 0$, sinks $b_v < 0$, and the supplies sum to zero.
:::

### 0.2 Linear programming and duality

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Primal and dual linear programs]{.tag} For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times q}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}^q$, the primal and dual programs are
$$
(P)\ \max \{ c^\top x : A x \leq b,\ x \geq 0 \}, \qquad (D)\ \min \{ b^\top y : A^\top y \geq c,\ y \geq 0 \}.
$$
Each dual variable $y_i$ is attached to one primal constraint.
:::

::: thm
[Lemma 0.4 — Farkas]{.tag} Exactly one of the two systems has a solution:
$$
\text{(i)}\ A x = b,\ x \geq 0; \qquad \text{(ii)}\ A^\top y \geq 0,\ b^\top y < 0 .
$$
Geometrically, either $b$ lies in the cone generated by the columns of $A$, or a hyperplane separates $b$ from that cone; the certificate $y$ is what Benders decomposition adds as a cut (ch. 5.5).

With slack variables, the inequality form follows: $A x \leq b$, $x \geq 0$ is infeasible if and only if some $y \geq 0$ has $A^\top y \geq 0$ and $b^\top y < 0$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Weak and strong duality]{.tag} If $x$ is feasible for $(P)$ and $y$ for $(D)$, then
$$
c^\top x \leq b^\top y .
$$
If $(P)$ has a finite optimum, so has $(D)$, and
$$
\max (P) = \min (D).
$$

::: proof
Weak duality is one line: $c^\top x \leq (A^\top y)^\top x = y^\top A x \leq y^\top b$, using $x \geq 0$, $y \geq 0$ and both sets of constraints.

Strong duality follows from the inequality form of Lemma 0.4. Let $z^\star = \max (P)$; it suffices to find a dual feasible $y$ with $b^\top y \leq z^\star$.

1.  If none exists, the system $A^\top y \geq c$, $y \geq 0$, $b^\top y \leq z^\star$ is infeasible, and Lemma 0.4 gives $x \geq 0$ and $\lambda \geq 0$ with
    $$
    A x \leq \lambda b, \qquad c^\top x > \lambda z^\star .
    $$
2.  If $\lambda > 0$, the point $x / \lambda$ is feasible for $(P)$ with value above $z^\star$, a contradiction.
3.  If $\lambda = 0$, then $A x \leq 0$ and $c^\top x > 0$: adding $t x$ to any feasible point improves it without bound as $t \to \infty$, which contradicts a finite optimum. Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis (1997, ch. 4) give the details. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — Complementary slackness]{.tag} Feasible $x$ and $y$ are both optimal if and only if, for every row $i$ and every column $j$,
$$
y_i \, (b - A x)_i = 0, \qquad x_j \, (A^\top y - c)_j = 0 .
$$

::: proof
The gap $b^\top y - c^\top x$ equals $y^\top (b - Ax) + x^\top (A^\top y - c)$, a sum of non-negative products. By Theorem 0.5, $x$ and $y$ are both optimal exactly when the gap is zero, that is, when every product vanishes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A dual variable is a **shadow price**: the rate at which the optimal value changes when the right-hand side of its constraint grows. In network models, the dual of a capacity constraint is the value of one more unit of capacity on that link (ch. 3.2, ch. 5.4).

::: ex
[Example 0.7 — Duality on a small LP]{.tag} Maximise $3x_1 + 2x_2$ subject to $x_1 + x_2 \leq 4$, $x_1 + 3x_2 \leq 6$, $x_1 \leq 3.5$ and $x \geq 0$.

-   The first and third constraints are tight at $x = (3.5, 0.5)$, of value $11.5$.
-   Complementary slackness forces $y_2 = 0$, since the second constraint has slack $1$.
-   The dual constraints then read $y_1 + y_3 = 3$ and $y_1 = 2$, so $y = (2, 0, 1)$.
-   The dual value is $4 \cdot 2 + 3.5 \cdot 1$, and both values agree:
$$
c^\top x = b^\top y = 11.5 .
$$
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

# Primal: max 3x1 + 2x2  s.t.  x1 + x2 <= 4,  x1 + 3x2 <= 6,  x1 <= 3.5,  x >= 0
c = np.array([3.0, 2.0])
A = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0], [1.0, 0.0]])
b = np.array([4.0, 6.0, 3.5])
res = linprog(-c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b, bounds=[(0, None)] * 2, method="highs")
x = res.x
y = -res.ineqlin.marginals          # dual prices (HiGHS reports d(min)/db)
print("primal x =", x, " value =", c @ x)
print("dual   y =", y, " value =", b @ y)
print("slack b - Ax =", b - A @ x, " y * slack =", y * (b - A @ x))
print("reduced costs A^T y - c =", A.T @ y - c)
```

The solver returns the primal and dual solutions of Example 0.7, and every complementary product is zero.

### 0.3 Integer programs and complexity

::: def
[Definition 0.8 — Mixed-integer program and LP relaxation]{.tag} A mixed-integer linear program (MILP) is
$$
z_{IP} = \min \{ c^\top x : A x \geq b,\ x \geq 0,\ x_j \in \mathbb{Z} \text{ for } j \in J \}.
$$
Its **LP relaxation** drops the integrality of the variables in $J$; its value is $z_{LP}$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.9 — The relaxation bounds the integer optimum]{.tag} For a minimisation,
$$
z_{LP} \leq z_{IP} .
$$
For any feasible integer solution of value $z_{UB} > 0$, the optimality gap $(z_{UB} - z_{LP}) / z_{UB}$ bounds how far that solution is from the optimum.

::: proof
Every feasible point of the MILP is feasible for the relaxation, so the relaxation minimises over a larger set. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The whole of ch. 4–5 is about making $z_{LP}$ close to $z_{IP}$ (strong formulations, cuts) and exploiting the gap (branch-and-bound).

::: def
[Definition 0.10 — P, NP and NP-hardness]{.tag} A decision problem is in P if an algorithm answers it in time polynomial in the input size. It is in NP if a “yes” answer has a certificate checkable in polynomial time. A problem is **NP-hard** if every problem of NP reduces to it by a polynomial transformation.
:::

Unless P = NP, an NP-hard problem has no polynomial algorithm. Deciding whether a MILP is feasible is NP-hard, and so are most network problems with integer decisions: the knapsack problem behind capacity upgrades (ch. 5.1), the Steiner tree problem behind network design (ch. 4.1), integer multicommodity flow (ch. 2.4) and the facility location problems of ch. 6 (Garey and Johnson, 1979).

NP-hardness is a worst-case statement. Modern solvers routinely solve network instances with thousands of binary variables, and the exact methods of ch. 5 exploit structure to go further. When the time budget is seconds, heuristics take over (ch. 7–10).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Flow conservation is $N x = b$, with the node–arc incidence matrix $N$.
-   LP duality: weak duality gives bounds, strong duality equality, complementary slackness certificates of optimality.
-   Dual variables are prices; Farkas' lemma gives certificates of infeasibility.
-   The LP relaxation bounds a MILP; the optimality gap measures the quality of any feasible solution.
-   Most network problems with integer decisions are NP-hard, yet often solvable in practice.
:::

## 1. Telecommunication networks and their optimization problems {#ch1}

An optimization model of a network needs four ingredients: a graph with capacities, a traffic to carry, a set of routing rules and a time scale for the decision. This chapter introduces them, with only the networking vocabulary the models use.

### 1.1 Layers, links and capacities

A backbone network is built in layers. The **optical layer** carries wavelengths on fibres (wavelength-division multiplexing, WDM). The **IP/MPLS layer** sees each wavelength, or each bundle of them, as one link between two routers.

Capacity is installed in **modules**: interfaces of 10, 100 or 400 Gb/s, wavelengths, fibre pairs. Its cost is therefore a step function of the volume, which is why capacity planning is an integer problem (ch. 4.4).

### 1.2 Traffic matrices

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Demand and traffic matrix]{.tag} A **demand** (or commodity) $k$ is a triple $(s_k, t_k, d_k)$: an origin, a destination and a volume in Gb/s. The **traffic matrix** $T$ collects the volumes $T_{st}$ of all origin–destination pairs, usually at the busy hour.
:::

Traffic matrices are rarely measured directly; they are estimated from link counts and sampled flows. The simplest model, often used as a prior, is the gravity model.

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Gravity model]{.tag} Given node weights $P_v > 0$ (population, number of customers) and a total volume $\tau$, the gravity traffic matrix is
$$
T_{st} = \tau \, \frac{P_s P_t}{\sum_{u \neq v} P_u P_v}, \qquad s \neq t .
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.3 — The six-node backbone]{.tag} The backbone of this page has nodes A to F and eight full-duplex links, all of 10 Gb/s except B–C and C–E, of 5 Gb/s:

-   links A–B, A–C, B–C, B–D, C–E, D–E, D–F and E–F;
-   weights $P = (4, 2, 2, 2, 2, 4)$ for A to F and a total of $\tau = 40$ Gb/s;
-   the normalising sum is $16^2 - 48 = 208$, so for instance
$$
T_{AF} = 40 \cdot \tfrac{16}{208} = 3.08 \text{ Gb/s}, \qquad T_{BC} = 40 \cdot \tfrac{4}{208} = 0.77 \text{ Gb/s}.
$$
:::

### 1.3 Routing

How traffic follows the links depends on the technology.

-   **Shortest-path protocols** (OSPF, IS-IS) give each link an administrative weight; every router forwards a packet along a shortest path to its destination. With **ECMP** (equal-cost multipath), traffic is split evenly among equal-length next hops. The operator controls the routing only through the weights (ch. 3.3).
-   **Explicit routing** (MPLS traffic engineering, segment routing) lets the operator choose the path of each flow, possibly with a few waypoints (ch. 3.4).
-   **Software-defined networking** (SDN) separates the control plane from the forwarding plane: a logically centralised controller computes the routes and installs them in the switches (McKeown et al., 2008). Where to place the controllers is itself a problem (ch. 6.2).

The quality of a routing is first measured by the **utilisation** of each link, load divided by capacity. Queueing delay grows quickly as utilisation approaches 1, so operators keep headroom below full load.

```python
import numpy as np, networkx as nx
links = [("A", "B", 10), ("A", "C", 10), ("B", "C", 5), ("B", "D", 10),
         ("C", "E", 5), ("D", "E", 10), ("D", "F", 10), ("E", "F", 10)]      # Gb/s
G = nx.DiGraph([(u, v, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links] + [(v, u, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links])
nodes, P = sorted(G), {"A": 4, "B": 2, "C": 2, "D": 2, "E": 2, "F": 4}
Z = sum(P[s] * P[t] for s in nodes for t in nodes if s != t)
T = {(s, t): 40 * P[s] * P[t] / Z for s in nodes for t in nodes if s != t}  # gravity, 40 Gb/s

# Route every demand on one minimum-hop path and accumulate the load of each arc.
load = dict.fromkeys(G.edges, 0.0)
for (s, t), d in T.items():
    path = nx.shortest_path(G, s, t)                    # fewest hops, first one found
    for a in zip(path, path[1:]):
        load[a] += d
util = {a: load[a] / G.edges[a]["cap"] for a in G.edges}
worst = max(util, key=util.get)
print("T[A,F] = %.2f Gb/s, T[B,C] = %.2f Gb/s, total %.0f Gb/s" % (T["A", "F"], T["B", "C"], sum(T.values())))
print("most loaded arc", worst, "utilisation %.2f" % util[worst])
```

The first lines of this block define the backbone; later blocks repeat them so that each one runs on its own. With one minimum-hop path per demand, the arc C→E carries 4.6 Gb/s on 5 Gb/s:

$$
\text{maximum utilisation} = 0.92 .
$$

Chapter 3 shows that a better routing of the same traffic exists, and how to prove that it is optimal.

### 1.4 Virtualization and autonomy

Three evolutions change the optimization problems.

-   **Network functions virtualization** (NFV) replaces dedicated boxes (firewalls, load balancers, packet gateways) by software, the virtual network functions (VNFs), running on servers in data centres. A service becomes a **service function chain**: an ordered list of VNFs that a flow must traverse (ch. 6.3).
-   **Network slicing**, central in 5G, shares one physical network among several logical networks, each with its own guarantees of throughput, latency or reliability (ch. 8.2).
-   **Autonomous networks** close the loop: monitoring, analysis, decision and configuration run without a human operator, so decisions must be computed in seconds or less (ch. 8.4).

### 1.5 Three time scales of decisions

| Time scale | Decisions | Typical model | Chapter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Years: design and dimensioning | which links and nodes to build, how many modules | MILP with fixed costs | ch. 4 |
| Months: capacity planning | upgrades for forecast traffic, protection capacity | MILP, decomposition | ch. 4–5, 9 |
| Minutes to milliseconds: operation and orchestration | routing, placement of functions, admission of slices | LP, fast heuristics, learned policies | ch. 3, 6–8, 10 |

The objectives also vary: installation cost, maximum utilisation, latency, energy, robustness to failures. A good model states which one matters and turns the others into constraints.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   A network model has a graph with capacities, a traffic matrix, routing rules and a time scale.
-   Capacities come in modules, so dimensioning and planning are integer problems.
-   Shortest-path protocols route through weights; explicit routing and SDN choose paths directly.
-   Virtualization adds compute resources and service chains; slicing and autonomy add guarantees and time limits.
-   On the backbone, one minimum-hop path per demand loads a link to 92 %.
:::

## 2. Flows, paths and cuts {#ch2}

Routing is a flow problem. This chapter solves the single-commodity problems in polynomial time, explains why their solutions are integral, and shows what breaks when several commodities share the capacities.

### 2.1 Shortest paths

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Shortest path problem]{.tag} Given arc lengths $w_a \geq 0$ and two nodes $s, t$, find a path from $s$ to $t$ of minimum total length. The distance $\mathrm{dist}(s, v)$ is that minimum for target $v$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Dijkstra's algorithm]{.tag} Keep a tentative label $\ell(v)$, with $\ell(s) = 0$ and $\ell(v) = \infty$ otherwise. Repeatedly make permanent the non-permanent node $u$ of smallest label, and relax its outgoing arcs:
$$
\ell(v) \leftarrow \min \big( \ell(v),\ \ell(u) + w_{uv} \big).
$$
With non-negative lengths, every permanent label equals the distance. A binary heap gives a running time of order $(n + m) \log n$.

::: proof
By induction on the permanent nodes, whose labels are assumed exact. Let $u$ be the next node made permanent and take a shortest path $P$ to $u$.

1.  Let $(q, r)$ be the first arc of $P$ that leaves the permanent set. Since $q$ is permanent, its arcs were relaxed, so $\ell(r) \leq \mathrm{dist}(s, r)$.
2.  Lengths are non-negative, so $\mathrm{dist}(s, r) \leq \mathrm{dist}(s, u)$, the length of $P$.
3.  Node $u$ was chosen with the smallest label, so $\ell(u) \leq \ell(r)$. Chaining, $\ell(u) \leq \mathrm{dist}(s, u)$, and a label is always the length of some path, hence equality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With negative lengths but no negative cycle, the Bellman–Ford algorithm relaxes every arc $n - 1$ times; a further improvement reveals a negative cycle.

The shortest path problem is also an LP: send one unit from $s$ to $t$ at minimum cost, $\min \{ w^\top x : N x = e_s - e_t,\ x \geq 0 \}$. Its dual has one **potential** $\pi_v$ per node:
$$
\max \ \pi_s - \pi_t \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \pi_u - \pi_v \leq w_{uv} \ \text{ for every arc } (u, v).
$$
Distances to $t$ are optimal potentials. Pricing in column generation (ch. 5.4) is exactly this problem.

### 2.2 Maximum flow and minimum cut

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — $s$–$t$ flow]{.tag} An $s$–$t$ flow is a vector $0 \leq x \leq c$ that satisfies conservation at every node other than $s$ and $t$. Its value is the net flow out of $s$:
$$
|x| = x(\delta^+(\{s\})) - x(\delta^-(\{s\})).
$$
An $s$–$t$ cut is a set $S$ with $s \in S$ and $t \notin S$; its capacity is $c(\delta^+(S))$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — Max-flow min-cut (Ford and Fulkerson, 1956)]{.tag} The maximum value of an $s$–$t$ flow equals the minimum capacity of an $s$–$t$ cut:
$$
\max_x |x| = \min_{S} c(\delta^+(S)).
$$

::: proof
1.  *Weak inequality.* For any flow and cut, summing conservation over $S$ gives
    $$
    |x| = x(\delta^+(S)) - x(\delta^-(S)) \leq c(\delta^+(S)).
    $$
2.  *Residual graph.* An arc $(u, v)$ has residual capacity $c_{uv} - x_{uv}$ forwards and $x_{uv}$ backwards. Pushing the smallest residual capacity along an $s$–$t$ path of the residual graph increases $|x|$.
3.  *Optimality.* Let $x$ be maximum and $S$ the nodes reachable from $s$ in the residual graph; then $t \notin S$. Every arc leaving $S$ is saturated and every arc entering $S$ is empty, otherwise more nodes would be reachable. Step 1 then holds with equality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Augmenting along shortest residual paths (Edmonds and Karp, 1972) terminates after at most $nm$ augmentations, whatever the capacities.

### 2.3 Total unimodularity and minimum-cost flows

::: def
[Definition 2.5 — Totally unimodular matrix]{.tag} A matrix is **totally unimodular** (TU) if every square submatrix has determinant $-1$, $0$ or $1$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.6 — Incidence matrices are TU]{.tag} The node–arc incidence matrix $N$ of a directed graph is totally unimodular.

::: proof
By induction on the size $k$ of a square submatrix $B$. Entries are in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$, so the case $k = 1$ holds.

For $k > 1$, each column of $B$ has at most one $+1$ and one $-1$.

1.  If some column of $B$ is zero, $\det B = 0$.
2.  If some column has a single non-zero entry, expand along it: $\det B = \pm \det B'$ with $B'$ of size $k - 1$, in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ by induction.
3.  Otherwise every column has exactly one $+1$ and one $-1$, so the rows of $B$ sum to zero and $\det B = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Corollary 2.7 — Integral flows]{.tag} If $A$ is TU and $b$, $c$ are integral, every vertex of $\{ x : A x = b,\ 0 \leq x \leq c \}$ is integral. In particular, the minimum-cost flow problem $\min \{ w^\top x : N x = b,\ 0 \leq x \leq c \}$ with integral supplies and capacities has an integral optimal solution, found by any simplex method.

::: proof
Once the variables at a bound are fixed, a vertex is the unique solution of a square non-singular system $B x_B = b'$, with $B$ a square submatrix of $A$ and $b'$ integral.

Total unimodularity gives $\det B = \pm 1$, and Cramer's rule writes each coordinate as an integer determinant divided by $\det B$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

So single-commodity problems with integer data are solved by linear programming, with integral answers for free. Maximum flow, shortest paths, transportation and assignment are all special cases.

```python
import numpy as np, networkx as nx
links = [("A", "B", 10), ("A", "C", 10), ("B", "C", 5), ("B", "D", 10),
         ("C", "E", 5), ("D", "E", 10), ("D", "F", 10), ("E", "F", 10)]      # Gb/s
G = nx.DiGraph([(u, v, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links] + [(v, u, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links])
ms = {("A", "B"): 2, ("A", "C"): 3, ("B", "C"): 1, ("B", "D"): 4,
      ("C", "E"): 2, ("D", "E"): 1, ("D", "F"): 2, ("E", "F"): 3}          # latency (ms)
for (u, v), w in ms.items():
    G.edges[u, v]["w"] = G.edges[v, u]["w"] = w

print("Dijkstra A->F:", nx.dijkstra_path(G, "A", "F", weight="w"),
      nx.dijkstra_path_length(G, "A", "F", weight="w"), "ms")
value, flow = nx.maximum_flow(G, "A", "F", capacity="cap")
cut_value, (S, Sbar) = nx.minimum_cut(G, "A", "F", capacity="cap")
print("max flow A->F =", value, "| min cut", sorted((u, v) for u in S for v in G[u] if v in Sbar), cut_value)

# Minimum-cost flow: 12 Gb/s from A to F, cost = latency x volume.
G.nodes["A"]["demand"], G.nodes["F"]["demand"] = -12, 12
f = nx.min_cost_flow(G, capacity="cap", weight="w")
print("min cost =", nx.cost_of_flow(G, f, weight="w"),
      "| integral:", all(float(x).is_integer() for u in f for x in f[u].values()))
```

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — Flows on the backbone]{.tag} With the latencies of the block (in ms), several paths from A to F tie at 8 ms. The maximum flow from A to F is 15 Gb/s, and the cut $S = \{A, B, C\}$ certifies it:
$$
c_{BD} + c_{CE} = 10 + 5 = 15 \text{ Gb/s}.
$$
Sending 12 Gb/s from A to F at minimum latency-weighted cost gives a cost of 96, with integral arc flows, as Corollary 2.7 predicts.
:::

### 2.4 Multicommodity flows

A network carries many demands at once, and they share the capacities. Let $K$ be the set of demands of Definition 1.1.

::: def
[Definition 2.9 — Arc-node formulation]{.tag} One flow vector $x^k \in \mathbb{R}^m_{\geq 0}$ per demand, with its own conservation constraints and a joint capacity constraint:
$$
N x^k = d_k (e_{s_k} - e_{t_k}) \quad (k \in K), \qquad \sum_{k \in K} x^k_a \leq c_a \quad (a \in A).
$$
It has $|K| \cdot m$ variables and a polynomial number of constraints.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.10 — Arc-path formulation]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{P}_k$ be the set of paths from $s_k$ to $t_k$, and $x_p \geq 0$ the flow on path $p$:
$$
\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_k} x_p = d_k \quad (k \in K), \qquad \sum_{k} \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_k : a \in p} x_p \leq c_a \quad (a \in A).
$$
It has few constraints but exponentially many variables, handled by column generation (ch. 5.4).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.11 — Flow decomposition]{.tag} Every flow $x \geq 0$ satisfying $N x = d (e_s - e_t)$ is a sum of at most $m$ flows, each along an $s$–$t$ path or a cycle. Hence the two formulations have the same LP optimum for any cost $w \geq 0$.

::: proof
While $x \neq 0$, follow arcs of positive flow from $s$, or from any node with positive flow if $|x| = 0$. Conservation guarantees an exit at every intermediate node, so the walk reaches $t$ or closes a cycle. Subtract the bottleneck value along it: at least one arc becomes zero, hence at most $m$ steps. With $w \geq 0$, dropping the cycles does not increase the cost. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Integrality is lost with several commodities: the constraint matrix is no longer TU, and the LP optimum can split a demand over paths with fractional volumes. Finding an integral multicommodity flow is NP-hard already with two commodities (Even, Itai and Shamir, 1976), and so is routing each demand on a single path (the unsplittable flow problem).

Feasibility is also subtler. The **cut condition**, that every cut has at least the capacity of the demands crossing it, is necessary but not sufficient. On the complete bipartite graph between $\{a_1, a_2\}$ and $\{b_1, b_2, b_3\}$, with unit undirected capacities and unit demands $a_1 a_2$, $b_1 b_2$, $b_2 b_3$, $b_1 b_3$, every cut satisfies it. Yet each demand needs a path of two edges, 8 units in total for 6 available: only 75 % of each demand can be routed.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.12 — Japanese theorem (Iri, 1971; Onaga and Kakusho, 1971)]{.tag} The multicommodity flow problem of Definition 2.9 is feasible if and only if, for every length vector $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^m_{\geq 0}$,
$$
\sum_{a \in A} \mu_a c_a \ \geq \ \sum_{k \in K} d_k \, \mathrm{dist}_\mu(s_k, t_k).
$$
These are the **metric inequalities**; cut inequalities are the special case where $\mu$ is the indicator of a cut.

::: proof
Necessity: route the flow on paths (Proposition 2.11); each unit of demand $k$ uses arcs whose lengths sum to at least $\mathrm{dist}_\mu(s_k, t_k)$, and the total length-weighted load is at most $\sum_a \mu_a c_a$.

Sufficiency: apply Lemma 0.4 to the arc-path system with slack variables on the capacities. Infeasibility yields multipliers $\mu_a \geq 0$ for the capacities and $u_k$ for the demands such that
$$
u_k \leq \sum_{a \in p} \mu_a \ \ (p \in \mathcal{P}_k), \qquad \sum_k d_k u_k > \sum_a \mu_a c_a .
$$
The first condition says $u_k \leq \mathrm{dist}_\mu(s_k, t_k)$, so the metric inequality for $\mu$ is violated. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The theorem is the bridge between routing and dimensioning: it describes the capacity vectors that can carry a traffic matrix without mentioning flows, which ch. 4.5 and Benders decomposition (ch. 5.5) exploit.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Dijkstra computes distances with non-negative lengths; distances are the optimal dual potentials of the shortest-path LP.
-   Maximum flow equals minimum cut; the residual graph gives both.
-   Incidence matrices are totally unimodular, so single-commodity flows with integer data are integral.
-   Multicommodity flows have arc-node and arc-path formulations with the same LP value, but lose integrality.
-   Feasibility is characterised by metric inequalities, not by cuts alone.
:::

## 3. Traffic engineering: routing the flows {#ch3}

Traffic engineering (TE) chooses how the traffic matrix is routed on a given network, so that no link is congested. This chapter states the usual objectives, solves the splittable problem by linear programming with a dual certificate, and then studies the routings that protocols can actually implement.

### 3.1 Congestion objectives

Let $\ell_a$ be the load of arc $a$, the total flow of all demands on it, and $u_a = \ell_a / c_a$ its utilisation.

-   **Maximum link utilisation** (MLU): minimise $\max_a u_a$. It keeps headroom for traffic surges and is a common objective of TE studies.
-   **Delay-like convex costs**: the M/M/1 queueing approximation gives a mean delay proportional to $\sum_a \ell_a / (c_a - \ell_a)$, which explodes near saturation.
-   **Piecewise-linear costs**: Fortz and Thorup (2000) charge each arc $c_a \, \phi(u_a)$, where $\phi$ is convex with slopes 1, 3, 10, 70, 500 and 5000 on the utilisation intervals cut at 1/3, 2/3, 9/10, 1 and 11/10.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.1 — Convex piecewise-linear costs are linear programs]{.tag} If $\phi(u) = \max_i (\alpha_i u + \beta_i)$ is convex and piecewise linear, minimising $\sum_a c_a \phi(\ell_a / c_a)$ over flows is the LP obtained with one variable $\Phi_a$ per arc and
$$
\Phi_a \geq \alpha_i \ell_a + \beta_i c_a \quad \text{for all } i, \qquad \min \sum_a \Phi_a .
$$

::: proof
For fixed loads, the smallest feasible $\Phi_a$ is the maximum of the affine pieces, which is $c_a \phi(\ell_a / c_a)$. Minimising over $\Phi$ and the flows jointly is therefore the same as minimising the original cost. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 3.2 Minimum maximum utilisation and its dual

::: def
[Definition 3.2 — MLU linear program]{.tag} With the arc-node variables of Definition 2.9 and one more variable $U$,
$$
\min U \quad \text{s.t.} \quad N x^k = d_k (e_{s_k} - e_{t_k}) \ (k \in K), \qquad \sum_{k} x^k_a \leq U c_a \ (a \in A), \qquad x \geq 0 .
$$
:::

For a splittable objective, demands with the same origin can be merged into one commodity with several sinks. This reduces the number of flow vectors from $|K|$ to $n$, which is what the code below does.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — The dual of MLU is a worst-case length function]{.tag} The optimal value of the MLU program is
$$
U^\star = \max_{\mu \geq 0,\ \sum_a \mu_a c_a = 1} \ \sum_{k \in K} d_k \, \mathrm{dist}_\mu(s_k, t_k).
$$
In particular, for every set of nodes $S$, with $d(S)$ the total demand from $S$ to its complement,
$$
U^\star \geq \frac{d(S)}{c(\delta^+(S))} .
$$

::: proof
A value $U$ is feasible when the capacities $U c$ can carry the traffic. By Theorem 2.12 this holds if and only if, for every $\mu \geq 0$,
$$
U \sum_a \mu_a c_a \geq \sum_k d_k \, \mathrm{dist}_\mu(s_k, t_k).
$$
Normalising $\sum_a \mu_a c_a = 1$ gives the formula.

For the cut bound, take $\mu_a = 1 / c(\delta^+(S))$ on the arcs of $\delta^+(S)$ and zero elsewhere. Every path from $S$ to its complement uses at least one of them, so demands leaving $S$ have length at least $1 / c(\delta^+(S))$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The optimal dual lengths $\mu$ are the shadow prices of the capacities: they say which links limit the network. As long as the same dual stays optimal, one more Gb/s on arc $a$ lowers $U^\star$ at the rate $U^\star \mu_a$.

```python
import numpy as np, networkx as nx
from scipy.optimize import linprog
links = [("A", "B", 10), ("A", "C", 10), ("B", "C", 5), ("B", "D", 10),
         ("C", "E", 5), ("D", "E", 10), ("D", "F", 10), ("E", "F", 10)]      # Gb/s
G = nx.DiGraph([(u, v, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links] + [(v, u, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links])
nodes, P = sorted(G), {"A": 4, "B": 2, "C": 2, "D": 2, "E": 2, "F": 4}
Z = sum(P[s] * P[t] for s in nodes for t in nodes if s != t)
T = {(s, t): 40 * P[s] * P[t] / Z for s in nodes for t in nodes if s != t}  # gravity, 40 Gb/s
arcs = list(G.edges); m, n = len(arcs), len(nodes)

# (a) Minimum maximum utilisation, splittable: flows aggregated by source, f[s, a] >= 0, plus U.
nv = n * m + 1
c = np.zeros(nv); c[-1] = 1.0
A_eq = np.zeros((n * n, nv)); b_eq = np.zeros(n * n)
for i, s in enumerate(nodes):
    for j, v in enumerate(nodes):
        for q, (a, b) in enumerate(arcs):
            A_eq[i * n + j, i * m + q] = (a == v) - (b == v)       # out minus in
        b_eq[i * n + j] = sum(T[s, t] for t in nodes if t != s) if v == s else -T.get((s, v), 0)
A_ub = np.zeros((m, nv))
for q, a in enumerate(arcs):
    A_ub[q, q:n * m:m] = 1.0; A_ub[q, -1] = -G.edges[a]["cap"]     # load_a <= U * c_a
r = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=np.zeros(m), A_eq=A_eq, b_eq=b_eq, method="highs")
mu = -r.ineqlin.marginals                                          # dual "lengths" of the arcs
print("LP optimum U* = %.3f | arcs with a positive dual:" % r.fun,
      [(arcs[q], round(float(mu[q]), 3)) for q in range(m) if mu[q] > 1e-9])

# (b) Shortest-path routing with unit weights and even splitting (ECMP).
def ecmp_load(w):
    load = dict.fromkeys(arcs, 0.0)
    for t in nodes:                                                # one destination at a time
        dist = nx.shortest_path_length(G.reverse(), t, weight=lambda u, v, d: w[v, u])
        inflow = {v: T.get((v, t), 0.0) for v in nodes}
        for v in sorted(nodes, key=lambda v: -dist[v]):           # farthest nodes first
            nxt = [(v, u) for u in G[v] if v != t and abs(dist[v] - w[v, u] - dist[u]) < 1e-9]
            for a in nxt:
                load[a] += inflow[v] / len(nxt); inflow[a[1]] += inflow[v] / len(nxt)
    return load
L = ecmp_load(dict.fromkeys(arcs, 1))
worst = max(arcs, key=lambda a: L[a] / G.edges[a]["cap"])
print("ECMP, unit weights: arc", worst, "utilisation %.3f" % (L[worst] / G.edges[worst]["cap"]))
```

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — The backbone is limited by one cut]{.tag} Take $S = \{A, B, C\}$, whose weights sum to 8, like those of its complement.

-   Traffic from $S$ to the complement: $40 \cdot 8 \cdot 8 / 208 = 12.31$ Gb/s.
-   Capacity leaving $S$: arcs B→D and C→E, $10 + 5 = 15$ Gb/s.
-   Theorem 3.3 gives $U^\star \geq 12.31 / 15$, and the LP reaches it:
$$
U^\star = 0.821 .
$$
-   The solver's dual puts the length $1/15 \approx 0.067$ on B→D and C→E and zero elsewhere: this is the cut of the theorem, an optimal dual solution.
:::

### 3.3 Shortest-path routing and the weight-setting problem

With OSPF or IS-IS, the operator does not choose paths: it chooses weights, and the protocol routes every packet on shortest paths for these weights, splitting evenly among equal-cost next hops (ECMP).

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Weight-setting problem]{.tag} Find integer weights $w_a \in \{1, \dots, w_{\max}\}$ such that the ECMP routing they induce minimises a congestion cost, such as the MLU or the Fortz–Thorup cost of ch. 3.1.
:::

Fortz and Thorup proved that finding optimal weights is NP-hard, and showed that local search on the weights comes close to the LP optimum on the backbones they studied (Fortz and Thorup, 2000; 2004). Not every routing is reachable this way.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Structure of shortest-path routings]{.tag} For any weights, the routing is destination-based (two packets for the same destination at the same node are forwarded alike), and every subpath of a used path is a shortest path between its endpoints. With ECMP, the split at a node is even among its shortest next hops.

::: proof
The set of shortest next hops of $v$ towards $t$ depends only on $v$, $t$ and the weights. If a subpath from $u$ to $v$ were not shortest, replacing it by a shorter one would shorten the whole path, a contradiction. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

On the backbone, unit weights send through the 5 Gb/s arc C→E all of the demands A→E, C→E and C→F, and half of A→F, B→E and C→D, that is 6.15 Gb/s. The block above confirms it:
$$
\text{ECMP with unit weights:}\quad u_{CE} = 1.231 .
$$
Even splitting is worse here than a single path (0.92, ch. 1). Ch. 7.3 tunes the weights by local search.

Complementary slackness explains why weights are powerful. In the min-cost multicommodity LP with capacity duals $\pi_a \geq 0$, every path carrying flow in an optimal solution is a shortest path for the lengths $w_a + \pi_a$. Wang, Wang and Zhang (2001) used this to show that optimal routings are shortest-path routings for suitable weights, provided the splitting ratios can be set freely rather than evenly.

### 3.4 Explicit routing and segment routing

**MPLS traffic engineering** sets up label-switched paths chosen by the operator. If each demand must follow a single path chosen among a candidate set $\mathcal{P}_k$ (for instance its $q$ shortest paths), the problem becomes a MILP with binary variables $z_p$:
$$
\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_k} z_p = 1 \ (k \in K), \qquad \sum_k \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_k : a \in p} d_k z_p \leq U c_a \ (a \in A).
$$
This is the unsplittable flow problem of ch. 2.4, NP-hard but solved well in practice for moderate sizes, or by rounding (ch. 7.2).

**Segment routing** (Filsfils et al., 2015) encodes a path as a short list of waypoints; between consecutive waypoints, packets follow the ECMP shortest paths of the protocol. With at most one intermediate waypoint per demand, TE stays an LP.

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Two-segment routing LP (Bhatia et al., 2015)]{.tag} Let $g_{uv}(a)$ be the fraction of the traffic from $u$ to $v$ that ECMP sends on arc $a$.

Variable $y_{k w} \geq 0$ is the share of demand $k$ sent through waypoint $w$, where $w = t_k$ means “direct”:
$$
\sum_{w \in V} y_{k w} = 1, \qquad \sum_{k} d_k \sum_{w} y_{k w} \big( g_{s_k w}(a) + g_{w t_k}(a) \big) \leq U c_a .
$$
:::

Bhatia and coauthors (2015) give such LPs for known and for uncertain traffic, and report maximum utilisations close to that of the fully splittable LP in their experiments.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   TE minimises the maximum utilisation or a convex congestion cost; convex piecewise-linear costs stay LPs.
-   The MLU optimum equals the worst normalised metric bound; any cut gives a lower bound and a certificate.
-   On the backbone, the cut $\{A, B, C\}$ proves that $U^\star = 0.821$ is optimal.
-   Shortest-path protocols route through weights; finding the best weights is NP-hard and even splitting can be harmful.
-   Explicit routing with candidate paths is a MILP; two-segment routing is an LP.
:::

## 4. Network design and capacity planning {#ch4}

Design decides which links to build; capacity planning decides how many modules to install on them. Both add integer variables to the flow models of ch. 2, and the quality of the formulation, not only its correctness, decides whether a solver can handle it.

### 4.1 Fixed-charge network design

Let $E$ be a set of candidate links, each with an opening cost $f_e$ and a capacity $c_e$ per direction; arc $a$ belongs to link $e(a)$.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Fixed-charge multicommodity network design]{.tag} With binary $y_e$ (link $e$ is built) and arc-node flows $x^k$,
$$
\min \ \sum_{e \in E} f_e y_e + \sum_{k \in K} \sum_{a \in A} w_a x^k_a
$$
subject to the conservation constraints of Definition 2.9 and the **weak linking constraints**
$$
\sum_{k \in K} x^k_a \leq c_{e(a)} \, y_{e(a)} \qquad (a \in A).
$$
:::

The problem is NP-hard: with zero routing costs, large capacities and demands from one root to a set of terminals, an optimal design is a minimum Steiner tree connecting them.

### 4.2 Strong and weak formulations

Two formulations with the same integer solutions can have very different LP relaxations. A demand that uses a fraction of a link only needs a fraction of its opening in the weak formulation.

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Strong linking constraints]{.tag} Add, for every arc and every demand,
$$
x^k_a \leq d_k \, y_{e(a)} \qquad (a \in A,\ k \in K).
$$
They are valid: a closed link carries no flow, and an open one carries at most $d_k$ of demand $k$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — The strong relaxation is tighter]{.tag} Let $Q_w$ and $Q_s$ be the LP relaxations with weak and with weak plus strong linking constraints. Then $Q_s \subseteq Q_w$, so
$$
z_{LP}(Q_w) \leq z_{LP}(Q_s) \leq z_{IP},
$$
and the first inequality can be strict.

::: proof
$Q_s$ has the constraints of $Q_w$ and more, so it is smaller and its minimum is larger.

For strictness, take one link with $c_e = 10$ and $f_e = 1$, one demand of 1 Gb/s and no routing cost. The weak relaxation sets $y_e = 0.1$, of value 0.1; the strong one forces $y_e = 1$, the integer optimum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

```python
import itertools, time
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import milp, LinearConstraint, Bounds
from scipy.sparse import lil_matrix

# Fixed-charge network design on 8 sites: which of the 28 candidate links to open?
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 8; xy = rng.uniform(0, 100, size=(n, 2))
E = list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 2))                       # candidate links
A = E + [(j, i) for i, j in E]                                      # both directions
length = {(i, j): np.linalg.norm(xy[i] - xy[j]) for i, j in A}
K = [(0, 7, 6), (1, 6, 4), (2, 5, 5), (3, 4, 3), (0, 5, 4), (6, 3, 2), (1, 2, 5), (4, 7, 3)]
cap, fixed = 10.0, 10.0                 # module capacity (Gb/s) and cost per km of an opened link

def model(strong):
    nx_, ny = len(A) * len(K), len(E)
    nv = nx_ + ny
    c = np.zeros(nv)
    for q, a in enumerate(A):
        for k in range(len(K)): c[k * len(A) + q] = 0.1 * length[a]   # routing cost per Gb/s
    c[nx_:] = [fixed * length[e] for e in E]
    rows_eq, beq = lil_matrix((len(K) * n, nv)), []
    for k, (s, t, d) in enumerate(K):
        for v in range(n):
            for q, (i, j) in enumerate(A):
                if i == v: rows_eq[k * n + v, k * len(A) + q] = 1
                if j == v: rows_eq[k * n + v, k * len(A) + q] = -1
            beq.append(d * ((v == s) - (v == t)))
    ub = []
    for q, (i, j) in enumerate(A):                                  # sum_k x_a^k <= cap * y_e
        e = E.index((min(i, j), max(i, j)))
        r = np.zeros(nv); r[[k * len(A) + q for k in range(len(K))]] = 1; r[nx_ + e] = -cap; ub.append(r)
        if strong:                                                  # x_a^k <= d_k * y_e
            for k, (_, _, d) in enumerate(K):
                r = np.zeros(nv); r[k * len(A) + q] = 1; r[nx_ + e] = -d; ub.append(r)
    cons = [LinearConstraint(rows_eq.tocsr(), beq, beq), LinearConstraint(np.array(ub), -np.inf, 0)]
    integ = np.r_[np.zeros(nx_), np.ones(ny)]
    lb, ubd = np.zeros(nv), np.r_[np.full(nx_, np.inf), np.ones(ny)]
    lp = milp(c, constraints=cons, integrality=np.zeros(nv), bounds=Bounds(lb, ubd))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    ip = milp(c, constraints=cons, integrality=integ, bounds=Bounds(lb, ubd))
    return lp.fun, ip.fun, ip.mip_node_count, time.perf_counter() - t0, int(round(ip.x[nx_:].sum()))

for strong in (False, True):
    lp, ip, nodes, sec, opened = model(strong)
    print("%-6s LP bound %7.1f | optimum %7.1f | gap %4.1f%% | B&B nodes %4d | %.2f s | links opened %d"
          % ("strong" if strong else "weak", lp, ip, 100 * (ip - lp) / ip, nodes, sec, opened))
```

::: ex
[Example 4.4 — Eight sites, 28 candidate links]{.tag} The block designs a network of 10 Gb/s links for eight demands. Both formulations reach the same optimum, 2363.8, with seven links opened. The difference is in the bound:

-   weak formulation: LP bound 1565.7, a root gap of 33.8 %, and 71 branch-and-bound nodes;
-   strong formulation: LP bound 2036.7, a gap of 13.8 %, and 7 nodes.

The strong model has more constraints but needs ten times fewer nodes (counts from SciPy 1.18; they vary with the solver version).
:::

### 4.3 A modelling toolbox

Real requirements are logical as much as linear. The standard linearisations, with binary $y, y'$, continuous $0 \leq x \leq M$ and a constant $M$ bounding $x$:

| Requirement | Linear constraints |
|---|---|
| $x > 0$ only if $y = 1$ (big-M) | $x \leq M y$ |
| at most $q$ of a set $J$ of options | $\sum_{j \in J} y_j \leq q$ |
| $y = 1$ implies $y' = 1$ | $y \leq y'$ |
| $z = y \, y'$ (both open) | $z \leq y$, $z \leq y'$, $z \geq y + y' - 1$ |
| $z = x \, y$ | $z \leq M y$, $z \leq x$, $z \geq x - M (1 - y)$, $z \geq 0$ |
| $U = \max_a u_a$ minimised | $U \geq u_a$ for all $a$ |

Big-M constraints are correct for any valid $M$ but weak when $M$ is large: the relaxation can set $y = x / M$, close to zero. Use the smallest valid bound, here the demand or the capacity, as in Definition 4.2.

### 4.4 Modular capacities and cut-set inequalities

In capacity planning the network exists; the question is how many modules to install. With an integer number $y_e \geq 0$ of modules of capacity $C$ on each link (shared by both directions here) and cost $\kappa_e$ per module, the **network loading problem** is
$$
\min \sum_{e} \kappa_e y_e \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \text{flows carry } T, \qquad \sum_{k} (x^k_{uv} + x^k_{vu}) \leq C y_e \ \ (e = uv),\ y_e \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.
$$

Its LP relaxation installs fractional modules exactly where needed and is weak. The classic remedy is to add cuts.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Cut-set inequalities]{.tag} For a set of nodes $S$, let $\delta(S)$ be the links with one end in $S$ and $D(S)$ the total demand between $S$ and its complement, in both directions. Every feasible solution satisfies
$$
\sum_{e \in \delta(S)} y_e \geq \left\lceil \frac{D(S)}{C} \right\rceil .
$$

::: proof
All demand between $S$ and its complement crosses links of $\delta(S)$, so $C \sum_{e \in \delta(S)} y_e \geq D(S)$. Divide by $C$. The left-hand side is an integer, so it is at least the rounded-up right-hand side: this is a Chvátal–Gomory rounding (ch. 5.2). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

On the backbone with $C = 10$ Gb/s and $S = \{A, B, C\}$, the demand across is $2 \times 12.31 = 24.6$ Gb/s. The LP relaxation can install 2.46 modules on the cut; the inequality demands 3. Barahona (1996) and Bienstock and coauthors (1998) used cut-set inequalities and their extensions to strengthen the relaxation of network loading problems substantially.

### 4.5 Metric inequalities and multi-period planning

Theorem 2.12 removes the flows altogether. With capacities shared by both directions, it holds with one length $\mu_e$ per link and the same proof. A capacity vector $C y$ carries the traffic if and only if
$$
\sum_{e} \mu_e \, C y_e \geq \sum_{k} d_k \, \mathrm{dist}_\mu(s_k, t_k) \qquad \text{for all } \mu \geq 0 .
$$
The **capacity formulation** minimises the module cost subject to these metric inequalities and integrality. There are infinitely many of them, but given $y$ a violated one is found by solving one multicommodity LP: this is Benders decomposition (ch. 5.5).

Planning is also dynamic. With forecast traffic matrices $T^1, \dots, T^H$ for successive periods, modules installed earlier remain, so the cumulative capacities satisfy $y^h_e \geq y^{h-1}_e$, and the cost of period $h$ is discounted. Delaying an installation saves money but risks congestion if the forecast is wrong, a trade-off revisited with robust models in ch. 9.2.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Network design adds binary opening variables to multicommodity flows; it generalises the Steiner tree problem.
-   Strong linking constraints $x^k_a \leq d_k y_e$ tighten the relaxation; on the example the gap falls from 33.8 % to 13.8 %.
-   Logical requirements linearise with binaries; big-M constants must be as small as possible.
-   Modular capacities make planning an integer program; cut-set inequalities round the capacity needed across each cut.
-   Metric inequalities give a formulation in capacities only, the basis of Benders decomposition.
:::

## 5. Exact methods: branch-and-bound, cutting planes and decomposition {#ch5}

A solver call hides several algorithms. This chapter opens the box: it enumerates cleverly (branch-and-bound), tightens the relaxation (cutting planes), and splits large models into easy pieces (Lagrangian relaxation, column generation, Benders decomposition), each on a network problem.

### 5.1 Branch-and-bound

::: def
[Algorithm 5.1 — Branch-and-bound for a minimisation MILP]{.tag} Keep a list of open subproblems, initially the MILP itself, and an incumbent value $z_{UB} = +\infty$.

1.  Select an open subproblem and solve its LP relaxation, of value $z$.
2.  If it is infeasible or $z \geq z_{UB}$, discard it (**pruning by bound**).
3.  If its solution is integral, update the incumbent if $z < z_{UB}$, and discard it.
4.  Otherwise pick a variable $x_j$ with fractional value $v$ and create two subproblems with $x_j \leq \lfloor v \rfloor$ and $x_j \geq \lceil v \rceil$ (**branching**).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Correctness]{.tag} If the integer variables are bounded, Algorithm 5.1 terminates. The final incumbent is optimal, and if none was found, the MILP is infeasible.

::: proof
Branching splits the feasible integer set of a node into two disjoint parts and loses no integer point. A node is discarded only if its LP, hence its integer set (Proposition 0.9), contains nothing better than the incumbent. Bounded integer variables can be branched on finitely often. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The search order matters. Depth-first search finds feasible solutions quickly and uses little memory; best-bound search processes the node of smallest LP value and minimises the number of nodes. Solvers mix both, and choose the branching variable by estimating the bound improvement (strong branching, pseudo-costs), a step that ch. 10.2 learns.

```python
import numpy as np
# Depth-first branch-and-bound for a 0-1 knapsack: choose link upgrades (value v, price w)
# within a budget W. The bound at a node is the LP relaxation, solved greedily (Dantzig).
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
n = 30; v = rng.integers(10, 60, n).astype(float); w = rng.integers(5, 40, n).astype(float)
W = 0.4 * w.sum()
order = np.argsort(-v / w); v, w = v[order], w[order]        # sort by value per unit of budget

def lp_bound(i, cap, val):
    """Value of the LP relaxation over items i.. with remaining budget cap."""
    while i < n and w[i] <= cap:
        cap -= w[i]; val += v[i]; i += 1
    return val + (v[i] * cap / w[i] if i < n else 0.0)

best, nodes = 0.0, 0
stack = [(0, W, 0.0)]                                        # (next item, budget left, value)
while stack:
    i, cap, val = stack.pop(); nodes += 1
    best = max(best, val)
    if i == n or lp_bound(i, cap, val) <= best:              # prune by bound
        continue
    stack.append((i + 1, cap, val))                          # branch x_i = 0
    if w[i] <= cap:
        stack.append((i + 1, cap - w[i], val + v[i]))        # branch x_i = 1 (explored first)
print("optimum %.0f | root LP bound %.1f | nodes explored %d of 2^%d = %d"
      % (best, lp_bound(0, W, 0.0), nodes, n, 2 ** n))
```

The knapsack models a budget of link upgrades, each with a value and a price. Thirty items have about $10^9$ subsets; with a root bound only 0.7 % above the optimum, branch-and-bound explores 118 nodes and proves the optimum, 761.

### 5.2 Cutting planes and branch-and-cut

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Valid inequality and separation]{.tag} An inequality $\alpha^\top x \leq \beta$ is **valid** for a MILP if every integer feasible point satisfies it. Given a fractional point $\bar x$, the **separation problem** finds a valid inequality violated by $\bar x$, or proves that none exists in a given family.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — Chvátal–Gomory rounding]{.tag} Let $\sum_j a_j x_j \leq b$ be valid for a set of non-negative integer vectors $x$. Then
$$
\sum_j \lfloor a_j \rfloor x_j \leq \lfloor b \rfloor
$$
is valid too. Every such inequality, derived from non-negative combinations of the constraints, is a **Chvátal–Gomory cut**.

::: proof
Since $x \geq 0$, $\sum_j \lfloor a_j \rfloor x_j \leq \sum_j a_j x_j \leq b$. The left-hand side is an integer, hence at most $\lfloor b \rfloor$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Gomory's fractional cut applies this rounding to a row of the optimal simplex tableau, and is violated by the current vertex. For a capacity row with binary variables, $\sum_j a_j y_j \leq b$, a **cover** is a set $J$ with $\sum_{j \in J} a_j > b$; the inequality $\sum_{j \in J} y_j \leq |J| - 1$ is valid, since not all of $J$ fits. The cut-set inequalities of Proposition 4.5 are problem-specific cuts.

**Branch-and-cut** separates cuts at the nodes of the tree. Together with presolve and primal heuristics, it is what modern solvers do: HiGHS (used here), SCIP, CPLEX and Gurobi.

### 5.3 Lagrangian relaxation

Some constraints link otherwise independent subproblems. In multicommodity flows, only the capacity constraints couple the demands.

::: def
[Definition 5.5 — Lagrangian relaxation]{.tag} For $z = \min \{ c^\top x : A x \leq b,\ x \in X \}$, where optimising over $X$ is easy, and multipliers $\lambda \geq 0$,
$$
L(\lambda) = \min_{x \in X} \ c^\top x + \lambda^\top (A x - b).
$$
The **Lagrangian dual** is $z_{LD} = \max_{\lambda \geq 0} L(\lambda)$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.6 — Lagrangian bounds]{.tag} For every $\lambda \geq 0$, $L(\lambda) \leq z$.

If $X$ is the set of integer points of a rational polyhedron, $z_{LD}$ is the minimum of $c^\top x$ over $Ax \leq b$ and the convex hull of $X$. Hence, if the subproblem has integral LP solutions,
$$
z_{LD} = z_{LP} .
$$

::: proof
For a feasible $x$, $\lambda^\top (A x - b) \leq 0$, so $L(\lambda) \leq c^\top x$. The characterisation (Geoffrion, 1974) follows from LP duality applied to the convex hull of $X$, which a linear objective cannot distinguish from $X$. If the LP over $X$ already has integral vertices, this hull is the LP polyhedron itself. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

$L$ is concave and piecewise linear. If $x_\lambda$ minimises the Lagrangian at $\lambda$, the violation $g = A x_\lambda - b$ is a **subgradient**:
$$
L(\lambda') \leq L(\lambda) + g^\top (\lambda' - \lambda) \quad \text{for all } \lambda' \geq 0 .
$$
The projected subgradient method updates $\lambda \leftarrow \max(0, \lambda + t_k g)$ with steps $t_k \to 0$ and $\sum_k t_k = \infty$. When the subgradients are bounded, the best value found converges to $z_{LD}$.

Relaxing the capacities of the min-cost multicommodity flow with multipliers $\pi_a$ leaves one shortest-path problem per demand, for the lengths $w_a + \pi_a$. The multipliers act as congestion tolls.

```python
import numpy as np, networkx as nx
links = [("A", "B", 10), ("A", "C", 10), ("B", "C", 5), ("B", "D", 10),
         ("C", "E", 5), ("D", "E", 10), ("D", "F", 10), ("E", "F", 10)]      # Gb/s
G = nx.DiGraph([(u, v, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links] + [(v, u, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links])
nodes, P = sorted(G), {"A": 4, "B": 2, "C": 2, "D": 2, "E": 2, "F": 4}
Z = sum(P[s] * P[t] for s in nodes for t in nodes if s != t)
T = {(s, t): 40 * P[s] * P[t] / Z for s in nodes for t in nodes if s != t}  # gravity, 40 Gb/s
ms = {("A", "B"): 2, ("A", "C"): 3, ("B", "C"): 1, ("B", "D"): 4,
      ("C", "E"): 2, ("D", "E"): 1, ("D", "F"): 2, ("E", "F"): 3}          # latency (ms)
for (u, v), w in ms.items():
    G.edges[u, v]["w"] = G.edges[v, u]["w"] = w
arcs = list(G.edges); cap = np.array([G.edges[a]["cap"] for a in arcs])

# Relax the capacity constraints with multipliers pi >= 0: the relaxed problem splits
# into one shortest-path problem per demand, for the arc lengths w + pi.
pi, best = np.zeros(len(arcs)), -np.inf
for k in range(300):
    for a, p in zip(arcs, pi):
        G.edges[a]["red"] = G.edges[a]["w"] + p
    load, value = np.zeros(len(arcs)), -pi @ cap
    for (s, t), d in T.items():
        path = nx.shortest_path(G, s, t, weight="red")
        value += d * nx.path_weight(G, path, "red")
        for a in zip(path, path[1:]):
            load[arcs.index(a)] += d
    best = max(best, value)                      # every L(pi) is a lower bound
    pi = np.maximum(0.0, pi + (load - cap) / (k + 1))   # projected subgradient step
print("best Lagrangian bound after 300 steps: %.3f" % best)
```

The subproblem is a set of shortest paths, which have integral LP solutions, so Theorem 5.6 predicts that the best bound is the LP optimum of the min-cost multicommodity flow; the next block computes it, 170.769, and the subgradient method reaches it within 300 steps.

### 5.4 Column generation

The arc-path formulation (Definition 2.10) has one variable per path. Column generation works with a small subset of paths, the **restricted master problem**, and adds the paths that can improve it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.7 — Pricing is a shortest-path problem]{.tag} Let $\sigma_k$ be the dual of the demand constraint of $k$ and $-\pi_a \leq 0$ the dual of the capacity of arc $a$ in the restricted master. The reduced cost of a path $p \in \mathcal{P}_k$ is
$$
\bar c_p = \sum_{a \in p} (w_a + \pi_a) - \sigma_k .
$$
The master solution is optimal for all paths if and only if, for every $k$, the shortest path for the lengths $w + \pi$ has length at least $\sigma_k$.

::: proof
The reduced cost is the cost minus the dual value of the column: $\sum_{a \in p} w_a - \sigma_k - \sum_{a \in p} (-\pi_a)$. An LP solution is optimal when no column has a negative reduced cost; minimising $\bar c_p$ over $\mathcal{P}_k$ is a shortest-path problem with non-negative lengths. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

```python
import numpy as np, networkx as nx
from scipy.optimize import linprog
links = [("A", "B", 10), ("A", "C", 10), ("B", "C", 5), ("B", "D", 10),
         ("C", "E", 5), ("D", "E", 10), ("D", "F", 10), ("E", "F", 10)]      # Gb/s
G = nx.DiGraph([(u, v, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links] + [(v, u, {"cap": c}) for u, v, c in links])
nodes, P = sorted(G), {"A": 4, "B": 2, "C": 2, "D": 2, "E": 2, "F": 4}
Z = sum(P[s] * P[t] for s in nodes for t in nodes if s != t)
T = {(s, t): 40 * P[s] * P[t] / Z for s in nodes for t in nodes if s != t}  # gravity, 40 Gb/s
ms = {("A", "B"): 2, ("A", "C"): 3, ("B", "C"): 1, ("B", "D"): 4,
      ("C", "E"): 2, ("D", "E"): 1, ("D", "F"): 2, ("E", "F"): 3}          # latency (ms)
for (u, v), w in ms.items():
    G.edges[u, v]["w"] = G.edges[v, u]["w"] = w
arcs, K = list(G.edges), list(T)
cap = [G.edges[a]["cap"] for a in arcs]

# Restricted master: path variables x_p, one artificial variable per demand (cost M).
cols = [(k, tuple(nx.shortest_path(G, *k, weight="w"))) for k in K]
for it in range(1, 50):
    n = len(cols)
    cost = [nx.path_weight(G, p, "w") for _, p in cols] + [1e3] * len(K)
    A_eq = np.hstack([np.array([[k == kk for kk, _ in cols] for k in K], float), np.eye(len(K))])
    A_ub = np.hstack([np.array([[a in set(zip(p, p[1:])) for _, p in cols] for a in arcs], float),
                      np.zeros((len(arcs), len(K)))])
    r = linprog(cost, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=cap, A_eq=A_eq, b_eq=[T[k] for k in K], method="highs")
    u, pi = r.eqlin.marginals, -r.ineqlin.marginals          # duals: demands, capacities
    for a, p in zip(arcs, pi):
        G.edges[a]["red"] = G.edges[a]["w"] + p
    new = [(k, tuple(nx.shortest_path(G, *k, weight="red"))) for k in K]     # pricing
    new = [(k, p) for i, (k, p) in enumerate(new) if nx.path_weight(G, p, "red") < u[i] - 1e-9]
    if not new:
        break
    cols += new
print("column generation: %d master solves, %d paths, cost %.3f" % (it, len(cols), r.fun))
```

Starting from one shortest path per demand, the artificial variables absorb what the capacities refuse; the duals then price the congested arcs, pricing adds 10 detours, and the second master is optimal: 40 paths and the cost 170.769 of the 480-variable arc-node LP. When paths must be integral (unsplittable routing), column generation is embedded in branch-and-bound: **branch-and-price** (Barnhart et al., 1998).

### 5.5 Benders decomposition

In capacity planning, fixing the capacities $y$ leaves a pure routing LP. Benders (1962) keeps $y$ in a **master problem** and lets the routing subproblem return cuts.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.8 — Benders feasibility cuts are metric inequalities]{.tag} Fix capacities $\bar y$. If the routing LP is infeasible, Lemma 0.4 returns arc lengths $\bar \mu \geq 0$ with
$$
\sum_e \bar \mu_e \, C \bar y_e < \sum_k d_k \, \mathrm{dist}_{\bar \mu}(s_k, t_k),
$$
and the metric inequality for $\bar \mu$, linear in $y$, is valid for every feasible capacity vector and cuts off $\bar y$.

::: proof
This is the sufficiency part of Theorem 2.12 applied to the capacities $C \bar y$. Validity is its necessity part. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The algorithm alternates: solve the master (minimise $\sum_e \kappa_e y_e$ over integer $y$ subject to the cuts found so far), test the routing, add a cut if infeasible. When routing costs matter, optimality cuts built from the dual of the routing LP are added as well. Each cut corresponds to an extreme ray or point of a fixed dual polyhedron, so finitely many cuts suffice. Costa (2005) surveys Benders decomposition for fixed-charge network design.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Branch-and-bound prunes with LP bounds; a tight root bound turns $2^{30}$ subsets into 118 nodes.
-   Chvátal–Gomory rounding, covers and cut-sets give valid inequalities; branch-and-cut separates them in the tree.
-   Lagrangian relaxation of capacities leaves shortest paths; its bound equals the LP bound when the subproblem is integral.
-   Column generation prices paths with lengths $w + \pi$; branch-and-price makes it exact for integer routing.
-   Benders decomposition keeps capacities in a master problem and receives metric inequalities as cuts.
:::

## 6. Placement of network components {#ch6}

Where should controllers, caches, gateways or virtual functions run? Placement problems are facility location problems on a graph, sometimes coupled with routing. This chapter formulates them and compares exact and greedy solutions.

### 6.1 Facility location

Let $I$ be the clients (switches, users, traffic sources), $J$ the candidate sites and $d_{ij}$ the cost of serving $i$ from $j$, typically a latency.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — $p$-median, $p$-center and facility location]{.tag} With binary $y_j$ (site $j$ is open) and $z_{ij}$ ($i$ is served by $j$):
$$
\min \sum_{i, j} d_{ij} z_{ij} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_j z_{ij} = 1,\quad z_{ij} \leq y_j,\quad \sum_j y_j = p .
$$
This is the **$p$-median** problem. The **$p$-center** problem minimises the worst cost $\max_i \sum_j d_{ij} z_{ij}$ instead. The **uncapacitated facility location** problem replaces the cardinality constraint by an opening cost $\sum_j f_j y_j$ in the objective.
:::

All three are NP-hard on general graphs. The constraint $z_{ij} \leq y_j$ is the strong form of linking, as in Definition 4.2; it makes the LP relaxation of the $p$-median often integral or nearly so on practical instances.

### 6.2 Controller placement in SDN

In a software-defined network, each switch talks to a controller. Heller, Sherwood and McKeown (2012) posed the controller placement problem: average latency leads to the $p$-median, worst-case latency to the $p$-center.

The simplest heuristic adds sites one at a time, each time the one that reduces the cost most. Its quality is understood through submodularity.

A set function $g$ is **submodular** when an element adds less to a larger set: for $S \subseteq S'$ and $j \notin S'$,
$$
g(S \cup \{j\}) - g(S) \geq g(S' \cup \{j\}) - g(S') .
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Greedy placement and submodularity]{.tag} For a set $S$ of open sites and a reference cost $d_{i0} \geq \max_j d_{ij}$, the savings function
$$
g(S) = \sum_{i \in I} \Big( d_{i0} - \min_{j \in S \cup \{0\}} d_{ij} \Big)
$$
is non-decreasing and submodular. Hence the greedy algorithm achieves at least $(1 - 1/e)$ of the maximum savings with $p$ sites (Nemhauser, Wolsey and Fisher, 1978).

::: proof
Monotonicity: adding a site can only lower each minimum.

Submodularity: for a client $i$, let $m_i(S)$ be its cost under the set $S$. Adding site $j$ gains $\max(0, m_i(S) - d_{ij})$ for this client.

If $S \subseteq S'$, then $m_i(S') \leq m_i(S)$, so the gain is smaller at $S'$. Summing over clients gives diminishing returns, and the cited theorem gives the ratio. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The guarantee is on savings, not on the cost itself; in practice greedy is often within a few per cent of the optimum. A swap-based local search (ch. 7.3) may improve it, but not always: Exercise 13 shows a greedy solution that no single swap improves.

```python
import numpy as np, networkx as nx
from scipy.optimize import milp, LinearConstraint, Bounds
from scipy.sparse import coo_matrix

# Controller placement as a p-median problem on a random geometric topology of 30 switches.
G = nx.random_geometric_graph(30, 0.3, seed=5)
for u, v in G.edges:
    G.edges[u, v]["ms"] = 10 * np.hypot(*np.subtract(G.nodes[u]["pos"], G.nodes[v]["pos"]))
D = nx.floyd_warshall_numpy(G, weight="ms")          # switch-to-switch latency (ms)
n, p = len(D), 3

def p_median(D, p, cand):
    """min sum_ij D_ij z_ij  s.t.  sum_j z_ij = 1,  sum_j y_j = p,  z_ij <= y_j  (sites in cand)."""
    n, m = len(D), len(cand); nv = n * m + m
    z = np.arange(n * m).reshape(n, m); y = n * m + np.arange(m)
    assign = coo_matrix((np.ones(n * m), (np.repeat(np.arange(n), m), z.ravel())), (n, nv))
    count = coo_matrix((np.ones(m), (np.zeros(m, int), y)), (1, nv))
    link = coo_matrix((np.r_[np.ones(n * m), -np.ones(n * m)],
                       (np.r_[z.ravel(), z.ravel()], np.r_[z.ravel(), np.tile(y, n)])), (n * m, nv))
    cons = [LinearConstraint(assign, 1, 1), LinearConstraint(count, p, p), LinearConstraint(link, -np.inf, 0)]
    r = milp(np.r_[D[:, cand].ravel(), np.zeros(m)], constraints=cons,
             integrality=np.r_[np.zeros(n * m), np.ones(m)], bounds=Bounds(0, 1))
    return r.fun, sorted(cand[j] for j in range(m) if r.x[y[j]] > 0.5)

opt, sites = p_median(D, p, list(range(n)))
chosen = []                                           # greedy: add the site that helps most
for _ in range(p):
    chosen.append(min((j for j in range(n) if j not in chosen),
                      key=lambda j: D[:, chosen + [j]].min(1).sum()))
greedy = D[:, chosen].min(1).sum()
print("optimum: sites %s, mean latency %.2f ms, worst %.2f ms" % (sites, opt / n, D[:, sites].min(1).max()))
print("greedy:  sites %s, mean latency %.2f ms (ratio %.3f)" % (sorted(chosen), greedy / n, greedy / opt))
```

::: ex
[Example 6.3 — Three controllers for thirty switches]{.tag} On a random geometric topology with link latencies proportional to distance:

-   the $p$-median optimum opens sites 12, 17 and 18, with a mean latency of 2.83 ms and a worst one of 6.15 ms;
-   greedy opens 11, 18 and 27, with a mean latency of 2.90 ms;
-   the greedy cost is therefore 2.4 % above the optimum, which the MILP certifies.
:::

### 6.3 VNF placement and service function chains

A service function chain is an ordered list of functions $(f_1, \dots, f_L)$ that the traffic of a request must traverse, for instance firewall, then load balancer, then cache. Each node $v$ offers a compute capacity $R_v$ (cores), each function $f$ consumes $r_f$ per instance, and links have capacities.

::: def
[Definition 6.4 — VNF placement and chaining]{.tag} Binary $y_{fv}$ opens an instance of function $f$ on node $v$ at cost $\gamma_{fv}$.

Binary $z^k_{\ell v}$ assigns the $\ell$-th function of request $k$ to node $v$, and flow variables route each segment of the chain. The model minimises opening plus routing costs subject to:
$$
\sum_v z^k_{\ell v} = 1, \qquad z^k_{\ell v} \leq y_{f_\ell v}, \qquad \sum_f r_f \, y_{fv} \leq R_v,
$$
flow conservation from the node of function $\ell$ to the node of function $\ell + 1$ for each segment, and link capacities shared by all segments.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.5 — Chain routing is a shortest path in a layered graph]{.tag} If the instances are already placed and capacities are not binding, the cheapest route of a chain is a shortest path in the graph made of $L + 1$ copies of the network, in which copy $\ell$ is joined to copy $\ell + 1$ by a zero-cost arc at every node hosting $f_{\ell + 1}$.

::: proof
A path from the source in copy 0 to the destination in copy $L$ must cross the $L$ layer arcs in order, each at a node hosting the next function. Projecting it onto the network gives a walk that visits the functions in order, with the same cost, and conversely. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The joint problem, placement plus routing with capacities, is NP-hard; MILPs solve instances of tens of nodes, and heuristics or decompositions handle larger ones (Herrera and Botero, 2016, survey the field).

### 6.4 Virtual network embedding

A slice or a tenant may ask for a whole virtual network: virtual nodes with compute demands, virtual links with bandwidth demands. **Virtual network embedding** maps virtual nodes to distinct physical nodes and virtual links to physical paths, within capacities, at minimum cost. It contains the unsplittable flow problem and is NP-hard (Fischer et al., 2013, survey it).

-   *Two-stage heuristics* map nodes first, greedily on available capacity, then route the links by shortest paths or multicommodity flows.
-   *Coordinated mapping* solves a relaxation of the joint MILP and rounds it (Chowdhury, Rahman and Boutaba, 2009).
-   *Path splitting*, when the substrate allows it, turns link mapping into an LP and raises the acceptance rate (Yu et al., 2008).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   Placement is facility location: $p$-median for mean latency, $p$-center for the worst case.
-   The savings of a placement are submodular, so greedy has a $(1 - 1/e)$ guarantee on savings.
-   On the example, greedy is 2.4 % above the optimum certified by the MILP.
-   VNF placement couples location, compute capacities and chain routing; with fixed placement, chains are shortest paths in a layered graph.
-   Virtual network embedding maps whole virtual networks; it is NP-hard and solved by staged, rounded or exact methods.
:::

## 7. Heuristics and matheuristics {#ch7}

When the instance is too large or the time budget too short for an exact method, a heuristic returns a good solution without proof of optimality. This chapter builds heuristics for the problems of ch. 3–6 and insists on measuring their quality against a bound.

### 7.1 Measuring a heuristic

A heuristic value $z_H$ means little alone. Three measures make it informative:

-   the **gap** to a lower bound $z_{LB}$ (LP, Lagrangian, cut bound), $(z_H - z_{LB}) / z_H$, which bounds the distance to the unknown optimum;
-   the **running time**, or the time needed to reach a target quality;
-   the **variability** over seeds and over instances of the same family, reported as a distribution, not a single best run.

A test set should contain instances of several sizes and structures, for example from SNDlib (Orlowski et al., 2010) or the Internet Topology Zoo (Knight et al., 2011), never only the instances used to tune parameters.

### 7.2 Constructive heuristics and rounding

**Greedy** algorithms build a solution step by step, choosing the locally best move: open the site with the largest saving (ch. 6.2), route demands one by one on the shortest path with enough residual capacity, largest demands first.

**LP rounding** solves the relaxation and rounds it. For unsplittable routing, Raghavan and Thompson (1987) choose for each demand one path at random, with the probabilities given by the path flows of the LP solution.

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.1 — Randomised rounding of path flows]{.tag} Let an LP solution route a fraction $x_p / d_k$ of each demand on path $p$, with load at most $c_a$ on every arc, and let every demand satisfy $d_k \leq c_{\min}$. Picking one path per demand independently with these probabilities gives an expected load at most $c_a$ on every arc. With high probability, every load is at most
$$
c_a \cdot O\Big( \frac{\log m}{\log \log m} \Big).
$$

::: proof
The load of arc $a$ is a sum of independent variables, one per demand, each between 0 and $d_k \leq c_{\min}$, and its expectation equals the LP load (linearity). A Chernoff bound for such sums bounds the probability that one arc exceeds its expectation by the stated factor by $1/m^2$; a union bound over the $m$ arcs concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In practice, rounding is followed by a repair step and a local search, and repeated with several seeds.

### 7.3 Local search and metaheuristics

::: def
[Definition 7.2 — Neighbourhood and local optimum]{.tag} A neighbourhood maps a solution to a set of nearby solutions: change one weight, swap one open site for a closed one, reroute one demand. A solution is a **local optimum** if no neighbour is better. Local search moves to a better neighbour until none exists.
:::

Metaheuristics escape local optima in different ways.

-   **Simulated annealing** (Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi, 1983) accepts a worse neighbour with probability $e^{-\Delta / \theta}$, where $\Delta$ is the deterioration and the temperature $\theta$ decreases over time.
-   **Tabu search** (Glover, 1989) moves to the best neighbour even if it is worse, and forbids undoing recent moves for a number of iterations.
